description: Religious experience, answered prayer, the design argument and Aquinas's First Three Ways as Christian evidence for God.
content_html:
Religious Experience as Evidence for God

Religious experience refers to moments when a person feels they have encountered God directly. The Bible records one of the most famous: in Exodus 3, Moses encounters God at the burning bush. A bush burns without being consumed; God calls Moses by name from within it and reveals his divine name and purpose. This experience transforms Moses from a reluctant fugitive into the leader of the Exodus. Christians point to the burning bush as evidence that God communicates directly with human beings and that these encounters have real, life-changing consequences.

Christians across denominations accept religious experience as a genuine route to knowledge of God. Atheists and Humanists challenge this, arguing that religious experiences are subjective inner states that could be produced by the brain, psychological conditioning, or wishful thinking. Richard Dawkins suggests the brain is wired to detect agency and meaning even where none exists. Christians respond that the moral transformation, lasting effects and consistency of religious experiences across vastly different cultures suggest they point to something beyond the individual mind.

Key Fact

Exodus 3 records Moses’s encounter with God at the burning bush — a bush that burned without being consumed. God spoke Moses’s name from the fire and commissioned him to lead the Israelites out of Egypt. Christians use this as evidence that God reveals himself through direct experience, not only through scripture or reason.

Prayer and Answered Prayer

Prayer is central to Christian life, and the experience of answered prayer is used by many Christians as evidence that God is real and responsive. 1 John 5:13–17 teaches that if Christians ask anything “according to his will,” God hears them and grants what they request. This is not a guarantee of receiving whatever is asked but a promise of God’s attentiveness to those who seek him. Christians who report praying for healing, guidance or provision and seeing specific outcomes often cite these experiences as among their strongest reasons for belief.

Atheists and Humanists are sceptical: they argue that apparently answered prayers are explained by coincidence, confirmation bias (noticing the hits and forgetting the misses), or the natural course of events. Studies on the efficacy of intercessory prayer have produced ambiguous results. Christians respond that reducing prayer to an experiment misunderstands its nature — prayer is not a mechanism for testing God but a relationship with a personal God who knows what is best. The claim is not that prayer guarantees specific outcomes but that God is personally present and active in the lives of believers who seek him.

Catholics and many Anglicans emphasise that prayer includes set prayers (the Lord’s Prayer, liturgical forms) that bind the Church across time. Protestant and evangelical Christians often emphasise informal, personal prayer as a direct conversation with God. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians frequently report dramatic answers to prayer including physical healing, which they present as evidence of God’s ongoing miraculous activity. Quakers traditionally practise waiting prayer — silence before God — which is about receptivity rather than petition. All these forms reflect the conviction that God is real and present, but the expectation of specific types of answer varies significantly.

The Design Argument

The design argument proposes that the universe’s order and complexity imply a designer. Paul states in Romans 1:18–24 that God’s “eternal power and divine nature” have been “clearly seen” in creation since the beginning of the world, making those who deny God without excuse. This gives the design argument scriptural support for Christians: the natural world itself testifies to God’s existence.

Paley’s watchmaker analogy from Natural Theology (1802) argues that if you found a watch on a heath, its intricate mechanism would lead you to infer a watchmaker. Living organisms are vastly more complex than any watch. Therefore, they too must have a designer — God. Many Christians find this persuasive: the fine-tuning of physical constants in the universe (the fact that even small changes would make life impossible) seems to point to intentional design.

The Cosmological Argument: Aquinas’s First Three Ways

The cosmological argument argues that the universe’s existence requires a cause beyond itself. Thomas Aquinas presented three forms in his Summa Theologica. His First Way begins from motion: everything moving was moved by something else; there cannot be an infinite chain, so there must be a first unmoved mover — God. His Second Way begins from causation: everything has a cause; there cannot be an infinite chain of causes, so there must be a first uncaused cause — God. His Third Way begins from contingency: things in the universe exist but might not have; there must be a necessary being whose existence is not dependent on anything else — God.

Atheists including Dawkins raise the “who made God?” objection: if everything requires a cause, God must also require a cause. Christians respond (following Aquinas) that God is by definition a necessary being — one who cannot fail to exist and does not require a cause outside himself. The cosmological argument does not say everything has a cause; it says everything that begins to exist or is contingent requires an explanation. Hume challenged whether the premise “every event has a cause” can be established by observation — we only observe causation within the universe, not the universe as a whole. Dawkins also argues that invoking God as the designer simply pushes the problem back: a designer complex enough to create the universe would itself require explanation. Christians respond that Dawkins conflates contingent complexity (which requires explanation) with necessary being (which does not).

Key Fact

Aquinas’s First Three Ways: (1) from motion — everything moved needs a mover, so there is an unmoved mover; (2) from causation — every effect has a cause, so there is a first uncaused cause; (3) from contingency — contingent things might not exist, so there is a necessary being. These are the spec content — the Ontological Argument (Anselm) is not assessed here.
exam_tip_html: This lesson covers four arguments in one — make sure you can write specifically about each one rather than blurring them together. The most dangerous error is confusing Aquinas’s Three Ways (a posteriori, from observation) with the Ontological Argument (a priori, from concept alone) — the latter is not on this course. For the 5-mark source question, Romans 1:18–24 is the named biblical anchor for the design argument: cite book, chapter and verse. For prayer as evidence, cite 1 John 5:13–17. For religious experience, Exodus 3 (burning bush). For the 12-mark Discuss, develop the Dawkins/Humanist counter-argument fully — one sentence is not enough. SPaG marks: cosmological, contingency, teleological, Aquinas.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Religious experience (e.g. Moses at the burning bush, Exodus 3) and answered prayer (1 John 5:13–17) are used by Christians as evidence that God is real and communicates with people; atheists argue these are subjective or coincidental.
  • The design argument (Paley’s watchmaker, Romans 1:18–24) argues natural complexity implies an intelligent creator; Dawkins counters that evolution explains complexity without a designer.
  • Aquinas’s First Three Ways (motion, causation, contingency) are a posteriori cosmological arguments for God as first mover, first cause and necessary being — distinct from the Ontological Argument (not on this course).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Aquinas's cosmological argument for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete features: everything in motion was moved by something else — there must be an unmoved first mover (1); every effect has a cause — there must be a first uncaused cause (1); contingent things might not exist — there must be a necessary being (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how the experience of Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3) is used as evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Moses encountered a bush that burned without being consumed (1); God spoke to Moses from the fire, calling him by name and revealing his identity (1); the experience transformed Moses and led him to a life-changing mission, suggesting it originated from a real divine source (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe answered prayer is evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Many Christians report specific outcomes that followed prayer — healing, guidance, provision — which they cannot explain except by God's action (2); 1 John 5:13-17 teaches that God hears those who ask according to his will, suggesting prayer involves real communication with a present and responsive God (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian reasons for believing the design argument supports the existence of God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The fine-tuning of the universe — physical constants are set so precisely that life would be impossible if they varied slightly — suggests intentional design by a creator (2); Romans 1:18-24 states that God's 'eternal power and divine nature' are 'clearly seen' in what has been made, providing scriptural support for the design argument (2); source credit for Romans 1:18-24 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Religious experience is the most convincing evidence that God exists.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: Exodus 3 (Moses), answered prayer (1 John 5:13-17), and the transforming effect of religious experience suggest genuine divine encounter. Counter: Dawkins argues experiences are brain-generated; Hume argues subjectivity means experiences provide no objective proof. Evaluate whether personal experience is stronger or weaker than philosophical arguments (design, cosmological). Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: religious experience, cosmological, revelation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which atheist and Humanist arguments challenge the design argument, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per challenge; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Darwin's theory of evolution (On the Origin of Species, 1859) shows biological complexity arises through natural selection without requiring a designer — Dawkins calls this a 'blind watchmaker' (2); the existence of suffering and 'bad design' (vestigial organs, disease, extinction) suggests that if the universe was designed, the designer is not all-loving and all-powerful (2); source credit for Romans 1:18-24 used in counter-framing, or Darwin cited explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What does 1 John 5:13-17 teach about prayer?
options: All prayers are automatically answered in the way the person expects
Prayer is only effective if performed in a church building
If Christians ask anything according to God's will, God hears and responds
Prayer is primarily about praising God, not making requests

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes Aquinas's Third Way?
options: Everything moving was moved by something else, so there must be an unmoved mover
Every effect has a cause, so there must be a first uncaused cause
Contingent things might not exist, so there must be a necessary being
The complexity of nature implies a designer

knowledge_checks.q: Paley's _____ analogy argues that just as a watch implies a watchmaker, so the complexity of nature implies a divine designer.
In Exodus 3, Moses encountered God in a bush that burned without being _____.
Match each argument to its key starting point:
right: The complexity and order of the natural world
Everything in motion was moved by something else
Contingent things might not exist — a necessary being is required

flashcard_questions.q: What does Exodus 3 record about Moses and religious experience?
flashcard_questions.a: Moses encountered God at a burning bush that was not consumed — God called him by name and commissioned him.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 1 John 5:13-17 teach about answered prayer?
flashcard_questions.a: If Christians ask anything according to God's will, God hears them — suggesting prayer involves real communication with a responsive God.
Just as a watch's complexity implies a watchmaker, so the complexity of living organisms implies a divine designer.

flashcard_questions.q: What scripture supports the design argument?
flashcard_questions.a: Romans 1:18-24 — God's 'eternal power and divine nature' are 'clearly seen' in what has been made.
From motion: everything moved was moved by something else, so there must be a first unmoved mover — God.
From causation: every effect has a cause, so there must be a first uncaused cause — God.
From contingency: things might not exist, so a necessary being (God) must exist to explain why anything does.
Natural selection produces biological complexity through random mutation and survival — no designer is needed.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the 'who made God?' atheist objection to the cosmological argument?
flashcard_questions.a: If everything needs a cause, God should too — Christians respond that God is a necessary being who doesn't require an external cause.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main atheist objection to religious experience as evidence for God?
flashcard_questions.a: Experiences are subjective and may be produced by brain chemistry or psychological conditioning, not by God.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'a posteriori' mean in philosophy?
flashcard_questions.a: Based on observation of the world — Aquinas's Three Ways start from observing motion, causation and contingency.

glossary_terms.definition: A direct personal encounter with what a person believes to be God or the divine, which may include overwhelming awe, a vision, or spiritual clarity.
Communication with God — whether spoken, silent, structured or spontaneous — through which Christians seek to encounter and respond to God.
A philosophical argument for God's existence based on the apparent order, complexity and purpose found in the natural world.
An English theologian (1743-1805) who argued in Natural Theology (1802) that the complexity of nature implies a divine designer.
Paley's analogy: just as finding a watch implies a watchmaker, so the complexity of living organisms implies God.
A philosophical argument for God's existence based on the existence of the universe, arguing it requires a first cause or necessary being.
In Aquinas's First Way, the being that initiates all motion without itself being moved — identified with God.
In Aquinas's Third Way, the observation that things might not exist — requiring a necessary being, God, to explain why anything exists at all.

hero_image_caption: The cosmos at night — used by Christians to support arguments from design and cosmological causation for God's existence
